questions.q: Which four reasons does this lesson give for why organizations invest in lineage?
options: Trust, impact analysis, root cause analysis, and audit/regulatory requirements
Faster internet speeds, cheaper storage, better branding, and fewer meetings
Smaller file sizes, prettier dashboards, shorter onboarding, and less code
Higher sales, lower taxes, improved morale, and fewer servers
questions.explain: The lesson's four reasons are trust (knowing where a number came from), impact analysis (checking dependencies before a change), root cause analysis (tracing a problem backward), and satisfying audit/regulatory requirements.

questions.q: In this lesson's example, why did three people independently check three different systems when a revenue number dropped?
options: Because nobody had a map of which systems actually feed that number
Because the company required three separate approvals for every number
Because the revenue number was stored in three different currencies
Because the dashboard software required three logins
questions.explain: Without a lineage record, nobody knew for certain which systems fed the number, so the investigation became exploratory and duplicated across people.

questions.q: How does this lesson define impact analysis?
options: Determining what downstream systems or reports would be affected by a proposed change, before making it
Measuring how much electricity a data center consumes
Counting how many users clicked on a report in the last month
Calculating the dollar cost of a software license
questions.explain: Impact analysis means checking dependencies in advance — for example, knowing a column feeds 6 downstream tables and 3 reports before renaming it.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what makes root cause analysis mechanical rather than exploratory when lineage exists?
options: You can walk backward through the recorded hops to the exact point where things diverged, instead of re-checking every system from scratch
The lineage tool automatically rewrites the broken code for you
Lineage eliminates the need for anyone to look at the data at all
Lineage guarantees that errors can never occur in the first place
questions.explain: Lineage turns a broad, uncertain investigation into a lookup — you check each recorded hop in order rather than guessing where to start.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect lineage back to the 'one definition, one home' idea from Metadata Management & Business Glossary?
options: Lineage proves that every report pulling a concept is pulling it correctly from its one home, through every hop, rather than drifting onto a stale copy
Lineage replaces the need for a business glossary entirely
Lineage and metadata management address completely unrelated problems
Lineage only applies to concepts that have never been defined in a glossary
questions.explain: The prior course solved identity (one definition, one home); lineage extends that to movement — verifying the path from that home to every report that uses it.
